title: Docker: build, run and diagnose
prerequisites: A terminal, Docker and a local checkout
summary: Read the actual Dockerfile, observe build caching, run Makan and diagnose a failed port mapping.
text:
## The problem

“It works on my machine” usually hides a difference: runtime version, installed packages, environment variables or file paths. An image packages the application and its runtime filesystem. A container starts a process from that image with isolation and resource controls. It shares the host kernel; it is not a small virtual machine with its own kernel.

Our goal is specific: build the Makan property service once, run it locally, then deliver that same image through CI and Argo CD. PostgreSQL holds the listings and viewing requests outside the application container. Replacing an application Pod must not erase a viewing request.

## In this repository

Open `nodejs/Dockerfile`, `nodejs/.dockerignore`, `nodejs/package-lock.json` and `nodejs/compose.yaml`. The Docker build context is `nodejs/`, not the repository root. These paths are relative to the repository checkout.

```dockerfile
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force && rm -rf /usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm
COPY --chown=node:node . .
ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV APP_VERSION=dev
USER 1000:1000
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

`FROM` chooses the runtime and base filesystem. This tag can move when its publisher updates it; a digest identifies immutable image content. CI gives our own application image a commit-based tag. Check the workflow rather than assuming a tag alone proves what is inside.

`WORKDIR` makes `/app` the working directory for following instructions and the startup command. `COPY package*.json` brings the dependency manifest and lockfile in before the application source. `npm ci` installs from that lockfile and fails if the manifest and lockfile disagree. `--omit=dev` leaves development packages out of the installed runtime dependencies.

Copying source later matters: a source edit can reuse the dependency-install cache. A lockfile edit invalidates that dependency step and the following steps. A cache is an optimization; the lockfile is the dependency record. Deleting npm from this image reduces runtime tooling, but it is not a substitute for vulnerability scanning or patching the base image.

`.dockerignore` keeps local dependencies, repository metadata and local environment files out of the build context. A secret copied into an image can survive in image layers even if a later instruction deletes it. Supply runtime secrets at runtime; do not add database URLs or administrator tokens to the Dockerfile.

`COPY --chown` controls ownership of application files. `USER` starts the service without root privileges. `EXPOSE` records the intended port; it does not publish a host port. The JSON form of `CMD` starts Node directly, so it can receive termination signals and close its HTTP server and database pool.

### Why not use a multi-stage build here?

This service runs plain JavaScript. There is no transpiled bundle or native application binary to copy out of a compiler stage. A single runtime stage is reasonable. Compare `golang/Dockerfile`: Go compiles in a builder stage, then the final image receives the executable and static web assets without the compiler. Add stages when they separate real build requirements, not simply to make every Dockerfile look the same.

### The data path

```text
Browser → published host port → Node container :3000
                                    ↓
                              PostgreSQL :5432
                                    ↓
                              named data volume
```

Inside Compose, the database hostname is the service name `database`. `localhost` inside the Node container means that Node container, not PostgreSQL and not your laptop. In Kubernetes, a Service provides the database hostname instead. The same application reads a different `DATABASE_URL` in each environment.

## Lab

Use a local checkout and Docker with Compose. This lab starts only local containers. From the repository root:

```sh
cd nodejs
cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env` and replace both placeholders. Use a password manager to generate a database password and a random administrator token of at least 32 characters. For this local URL, use a URL-safe database password. Do not commit `.env`.

```sh
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose ps
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/properties
```

Expect both health checks to return HTTP 200. The catalog contains six fictional homes on a new database. Open the site, filter by Maadi, open a home and submit a viewing request using sample contact details. Open the agent workspace and use your local administrator token to see the stored request. Change its status to `contacted`.

### Prove persistence rather than assuming it

```sh
docker compose restart app
```

Refresh the agent workspace and unlock it again if needed. The request and its status should still exist. The app process was replaced; the data stayed in PostgreSQL. A browser success message alone is not evidence of durable storage.

```sh
docker compose stop database
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz
```

The existing Node process should remain alive, so liveness stays 200. Readiness should fail with 503 because the database cannot answer. A live process cannot necessarily serve business requests. Kubernetes should stop sending normal traffic to an unready Pod, rather than continually restarting it for an unavailable dependency.

```sh
docker compose start database
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz
```

Retry readiness after the database starts. Expect recovery without rebuilding the application.

### Observe the build cache

```sh
docker build --progress=plain -t makan:lab .
docker build --progress=plain -t makan:lab .
```

The second build should reuse unchanged steps. Edit a visible sentence in `web/index.html`, rebuild, and identify the first invalidated step. Dependency installation should remain cached. Undo only your sentence edit afterward; do not discard unrelated local changes.

### Intentionally publish the wrong port

Temporarily change only the app port mapping in `compose.yaml` to `127.0.0.1:18080:9999`, keeping the valid database configuration. Recreate the app:

```sh
docker compose up -d app
curl --max-time 3 -i http://127.0.0.1:18080/healthz
docker compose logs --tail=30 app
```

Expect the HTTP request to fail even though the app can start. The process listens on 3000; publishing 9999 forwards to a port with no listener. Restore `127.0.0.1:3000:3000` and recreate the app. Change one variable at a time when diagnosing a real incident.

### Inspect runtime evidence

```sh
docker compose exec app id
docker compose exec app sh -c 'tr "\0" " " < /proc/1/cmdline'
docker compose logs --tail=30 app
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/metrics
```

The user should be non-root and process 1 should run Node. Request logs contain a generated request ID and route, without contact details or tokens. Metrics use route templates rather than property slugs or request IDs, keeping the number of label combinations bounded.

### Cleanup

```sh
docker compose down
```

The named database volume is retained. Use `docker compose down -v` only when you intend to delete this lab's database, including viewing requests. A volume is persistence, not a backup. A separate backup and a tested restore address a different failure.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | First evidence | Likely next check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Image fails to build | First failing Docker build step | Lockfile consistency, registry access, build context |
| App exits at startup | App logs and required configuration | Database health, URL and administrator token length |
| Health works, catalog fails | Readiness and HTTP status | Database connectivity and initialized schema |
| Connection refused from laptop | Published mapping in Compose | Host port versus actual container listener |
| New file is absent | Rebuild output and running image | Build context, ignored files, old container |
| Request disappears after restart | Database volume and target database | Whether you recreated the volume or connected to another database |

Do not print `.env`, dump container environments into a ticket, or paste connection strings into public logs. You can verify whether configuration is present without exposing its value.

## Verify your understanding

1. Explain why `EXPOSE 3000` alone does not let your browser reach the app.
2. Show which build step reruns after a source edit and explain why the dependency step can be reused.
3. Demonstrate a viewing request surviving an app restart.
4. Demonstrate liveness succeeding while readiness fails during a database outage.
5. Explain why three application replicas need one shared database rather than three in-memory request lists.

Evidence to keep: build output, HTTP status codes, and a redacted request reference before and after restart. You have completed the lab when you can reproduce and explain these outcomes, not when you have copied all the commands.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ Image بتجهز التطبيق، والـ Container بيشغّله. الداتا مكانها قاعدة بيانات مستقلة. اتأكد من الفرق بين البورت المنشور وبورت التطبيق، وبين العملية الشغالة والخدمة الجاهزة، واثبت إن الطلب فضل موجود بعد إعادة التشغيل.

## Sources

- [Docker build cache](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/)
- [Dockerfile reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/)
- [Docker Compose networking](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/networking/)

title: Git: ship a change you can undo
summary: Make a focused branch, inspect a diff, resolve a conflict and revert a change without rewriting shared history.
text:
## The problem

A deployment is easier to trust when you can answer three questions: what changed, who reviewed it, and how to undo it. Git records source history; it does not test your application or deploy Kubernetes objects by itself. Those jobs belong to the workflow and Argo CD.

A branch names a line of development. A commit records a snapshot and its parent history. A pull request is the review conversation around the proposed difference. A clean commit is useful because a reviewer and a future operator can understand one decision without reconstructing unrelated edits.

## In this repository

Read `.github/workflows/automate-build-apps.yml`, `charts/values-node.yaml` and `argocd/apps/nodejs.yaml`.

```text
Application commit → CI tests/build → image tagged with commit identity
                                    ↓
                         promotion updates Helm values
                                    ↓
                       Argo CD reconciles the cluster
```

The source commit, image reference and promotion commit are related but distinct records. A successful source build does not prove the new image has been promoted. A promotion commit does not prove the Pods have become Ready. Inspect evidence at each handoff.

A feature branch does not automatically become a production release. Check workflow event filters and the Argo CD target revision. Here, the deployment application follows `main`, and promotion changes the image tag in values.

## Lab

First inspect your working tree. Do not use reset commands to make existing work disappear.

```sh
git status --short
git log -5 --oneline
```

For practice, use a separate temporary repository so this exercise cannot accidentally promote a change to the platform:

```sh
mkdir git-delivery-lab
cd git-delivery-lab
git init -b main
git config user.name "Lab Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
printf 'Viewing requests are open.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git commit -m "Add viewing message"
git switch -c improve-message
printf 'Request a viewing from the property page.\n' > message.txt
git diff --check
git diff
```

`git diff` shows unstaged edits. It does not show what you have already staged. Stage the exact file and inspect the proposed snapshot:

```sh
git add message.txt
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Clarify how to request a viewing"
git log --oneline --all --graph
```

### Create and resolve a real conflict

```sh
git switch main
printf 'Contact the agent to arrange a visit.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git commit -m "Update agent contact wording"
git merge improve-message
```

Both branches changed the same original line. Expect a conflict, not a completed merge. Open `message.txt`, inspect the conflict markers and decide the final wording. Git cannot decide product intent for you.

```sh
printf 'Request a viewing from the property page; an agent will review it.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Merge clearer viewing instructions"
git status --short
```

The working tree should be clean. If you wanted to abandon the merge before resolving it, `git merge --abort` would return to the pre-merge state when possible. Do not continue issuing new merges while an unresolved merge is in progress.

### Undo a published-style change

Create one deliberately poor change, then reverse it with a new commit:

```sh
printf 'Viewing requests are permanently closed.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git commit -m "Close viewing requests"
git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log -3 --oneline
cat message.txt
```

The last commit reverses the bad change while keeping the record. This is why `revert` is often appropriate for history others already share. A reset can move a local branch pointer; force-pushing rewritten shared history changes what colleagues see. These are different operations with different consequences.

### Connect this to GitOps rollback

Suppose the application is failing after an image promotion. Find the promotion commit and its values diff. A reviewed revert of that promotion can ask Argo CD to reconcile the previous image reference. Editing a live Deployment alone may be undone by self-heal.

Before reverting, check compatibility: an older application may not understand a newer database schema. Git can reverse a manifest edit; it cannot automatically reverse data writes or make an unsafe migration compatible.

### Cleanup

The temporary `git-delivery-lab` directory is the whole exercise. Keep it for reference or remove that directory after verifying its path. Nothing from this lab needs to be pushed.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Inspect | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commit contains an unrelated file | `git diff --cached --stat` | Unstage that file, then review again |
| Your edit is missing from a commit | `git diff` and `git diff --cached` | Stage the intended edit |
| Merge does not finish | `git status` | Resolve each conflict or abort the merge |
| CI passes but site is unchanged | Image tag and promotion diff | Trace promotion and Argo CD status |
| Live fix disappears | Git desired state and Argo events | Commit the intended configuration |

## Verify your understanding

Explain the difference between an unstaged edit, a staged snapshot and a commit. Show a resolved conflict with the intended final wording. Show the bad commit and its separate revert. Finally, identify the file that records the Node image tag in the real repository and explain why a source commit alone is not proof of a completed release.

## Arabic takeaway

Git سجل للتغييرات، مش نظام نشر لوحده. راجع الـ diff قبل الـ commit، وحل التعارض بناءً على المعنى. الرجوع في GitOps يبدأ من الحالة المطلوبة في الريبو، مع مراجعة توافق التطبيق وقاعدة البيانات.

## Sources

- [Git: recording changes](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Recording-Changes-to-the-Repository)
- [Git: basic branching and merging](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging)
- [Git revert](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert)
- [Argo CD automated sync](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/auto_sync/)

title: Cilium, Flannel and NetworkPolicy
prerequisites: kubectl, a disposable cluster with a policy-capable CNI
summary: Separate networking from ingress, test isolation and restore only the traffic your service needs.
text:
## The problem

A working network is not automatically an appropriately restricted network. A frontend needs to reach an API; that does not mean every Pod should be able to reach a database or send traffic to the internet.

Separate the questions first. A CNI connects Pods. A Service supplies a stable destination for selected backends. An ingress controller handles incoming application routing. A NetworkPolicy describes which selected Pod connections are allowed. DNS resolves names; it does not grant permission to connect.

## In this repository

Read `networking/cilium/values.yaml`, `terraform/cilium.tf`, `networking/policies/applications.yaml`, `traefik/values.yaml`, `networking/metallb/address-pool.yaml` and `golang/deploy/chart/templates/network-policy.yaml`.

```text
External browser → advertised service address → Traefik → Service → application
                                                                  ↓
                                                          database Service

Cilium: Pod connectivity and policy enforcement
MetalLB: advertise service addresses in this environment
Traefik: HTTP routing and TLS entry point
NetworkPolicy: permitted Pod traffic, not HTTP page routing
```

The learning namespace has policies for application, database, identity and monitoring traffic. The older default-namespace application policy has a broader namespace-based ingress rule. These are different scopes; do not assume every workload uses the same policy just because it is in this repository. Selectors and namespaces decide which Pods a policy actually affects.

### Why Cilium rather than Flannel?

The repository records Cilium, VXLAN tunnelling and standard NetworkPolicy. That supports a clear present-day requirement: Pod connectivity plus policy enforcement. It does not record the original selection discussion, so we cannot claim a historical benchmark or migration reason that we have not measured.

| Option | What it supplies | Tradeoff for this lab |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flannel on its own | A network fabric connecting containers across hosts | Network policy enforcement requires another component |
| Cilium | Pod networking plus standard NetworkPolicy and additional Cilium-specific policy capabilities | More features and operational concepts to understand |
| Another policy-capable CNI | An alternative implementation of networking and enforcement | Evaluate compatibility, operations, visibility and measured requirements |

Flannel is not “bad networking.” Simpler connectivity can be a valid requirement. Cilium fits the current policy exercises without adding a separate enforcement component. Do not justify it with “we need eBPF” unless you can name and demonstrate the capability you actually need. Likewise, Hubble availability must be verified from configuration; installing Cilium does not prove every observability feature is enabled.

The manifests here use standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Avoid switching to Cilium-specific resources until a required capability calls for them; portability and a smaller conceptual surface are useful.

### Read a policy accurately

`podSelector` selects target Pods in the policy's namespace. Once a Pod is selected for ingress isolation, permitted ingress is the union of matching allow rules from applicable policies. Egress isolation is separate. For a connection between two isolated Pods, the source egress and destination ingress must both allow it. Policies are additive; an empty allow list in one policy does not override an allow in another.

A `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` in the same list item combine requirements. Separate list items offer alternative sources or destinations. Indentation can therefore change security meaning while still producing valid YAML.

## Lab

Use a disposable cluster with a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy. Merely accepting the resource through the Kubernetes API is not proof of enforcement. This lab creates an isolated namespace and does not modify platform policies. Confirm the current context first:

```sh
kubectl config current-context
kubectl create namespace policy-lab
kubectl -n policy-lab create deployment web --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl -n policy-lab expose deployment web --port=80
kubectl -n policy-lab run allowed --image=busybox:1.37 --labels=access=web --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n policy-lab run blocked --image=busybox:1.37 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n policy-lab rollout status deployment/web --timeout=90s
kubectl -n policy-lab wait --for=condition=Ready pod/allowed pod/blocked --timeout=90s
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec blocked -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
```

Both clients should reach the nginx page initially. If not, fix baseline scheduling, image pulling, Service endpoints or DNS before testing policy. A failed baseline cannot prove isolation.

### Isolate the server

Save this as `deny-web.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: isolate-web
  namespace: policy-lab
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress: []
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f deny-web.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec blocked -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
```

After enforcement converges, expect both new connections to time out. The Service still exists and the server can still be Ready. The connection is denied before it reaches the HTTP application. If both succeed, inspect labels, other policies and CNI enforcement; do not declare success based on `kubectl apply`.

### Allow only the labelled client

Save as `allow-web.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-labelled-client
  namespace: policy-lab
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              access: web
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 80
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f allow-web.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec blocked -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab get networkpolicy
```

Expect the allowed client to succeed and the blocked client to time out. The isolation policy still exists. The new allow policy adds a permitted source; it does not need to delete the isolation resource.

### Isolate client egress, then restore the necessary paths

Save as `client-egress.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: client-egress
  namespace: policy-lab
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      access: web
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress: []
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f client-egress.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- nslookup web
```

Expect name resolution to fail: egress to DNS is now blocked too. Edit `egress` to the following and reapply:

```yaml
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 80
```

Before applying, confirm your cluster's DNS Pod labels and namespace. This example assumes CoreDNS behind the usual kube-dns Service; NodeLocal DNS or different CNI handling may require a different destination rule. The policy must match the actual packet path.

```sh
kubectl apply -f client-egress.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- nslookup web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
```

Expect resolution and the permitted HTTP request to work. You restored two separate dependencies. Opening all egress would conceal which dependency was missing.

### Cleanup

```sh
kubectl delete namespace policy-lab
```

This deletes all resources in the dedicated lab namespace. Do not substitute a namespace containing your real application.

## Troubleshooting

| Evidence | Interpretation to investigate |
| --- | --- |
| Name cannot resolve | DNS itself may be blocked or unavailable |
| Name resolves, new connection times out | Source egress, destination ingress, routes or unavailable endpoints |
| HTTP 404 or 500 | A server answered; investigate routing or the application |
| Policy exists but traffic is unchanged | Target labels, namespace, other allow policies and CNI enforcement |
| Allowed client fails after egress isolation | Both source egress and server ingress need to allow the connection |

Inspect `kubectl get pods --show-labels`, `kubectl get networkpolicy -o yaml` and `kubectl get endpointslice` in the lab namespace. If available, Cilium flow visibility can add evidence, but the lab must still be explainable without assuming an installed dashboard.

## Verify your understanding

Keep a four-row result table: baseline, ingress isolation, labelled allow, and restored egress. For each, record whether DNS works and whether each client's HTTP connection works. Explain why Flannel alone does not meet the policy enforcement requirement, and why Traefik does not replace a CNI. Finally, identify a real source-to-destination rule in this repository and explain every selector and port.

## Arabic takeaway

Cilium بيوصل الـ Pods وبيطبق السياسات؛ Traefik بيوجه طلبات الويب، وMetalLB بيعلن عنوان الخدمة. الـ NetworkPolicy لازم تتجرب باتصال مسموح واتصال ممنوع، ومينفعش ننسى DNS. اختيار Cilium مناسب لمتطلباتنا الحالية، مش دليل إن البدائل وحشة.

## Sources

- [Kubernetes NetworkPolicy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/)
- [Cilium policy support](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/kubernetes/policy/)
- [Flannel project and networking scope](https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel#networking-details)
